units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. I'm putting the owner count away for this chapter.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Good idea. This one is hard.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: On the second of August, 1914, German soldiers crossed the border into Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By road and by rail. They seized the capital's railway station and the key bridges within hours.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a plain violation of the treaty of 1867.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Germany claimed it was only protecting the railways, which were vital to its plan to invade France through Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Luxembourg could do nothing.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The government protested, but it had no army worth the name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A popular story says that the young Grand Duchess Marie-Adélaïde drove to the Adolphe Bridge and tried to block it with her car.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Whether or not that's exactly true, it captures the helplessness of the moment.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A country that had trusted a piece of paper for fifty years was now occupied.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What was the occupation like?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Strange. Germany let the Luxembourg government keep operating, and promised not to harm the country.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the economy was tied into the German war machine, food grew scarce, and thousands of young men slipped away to join the French army, fighting under the French flag against the occupiers of their homeland.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Grand Duchess?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She was in an impossible position.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very young, very Catholic, very conservative.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She stayed in the country and kept up official contacts with the occupiers, including meeting the German Crown Prince.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that came back to haunt her.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When the war ended in November 1918, France and Belgium especially accused her of being pro-German.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Crowds demonstrated against her, and the French and the Americans refused to deal with her.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So she stepped down.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In January 1919, she abdicated in favor of her younger sister Charlotte, who was twenty-two.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Marie-Adélaïde left the country, entered a convent in Italy, and died in 1924, aged only twenty-nine.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the monarchy itself was now in question.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In September 1919, Luxembourgers voted in a double referendum.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The first question asked whether they wanted to keep the dynasty, and about seventy-eight percent said yes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The second asked what kind of economic union they wanted with a larger neighbor, and about seventy-three percent chose France.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And France said no.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So Luxembourg turned to Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1921, the two formed an economic union, with a shared customs area and a Luxembourg franc tied to the Belgian franc.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It lasted until both countries adopted the euro.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And 1919 brought a political revolution, too.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A revised constitution introduced universal suffrage, including women.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That year, women voted in Luxembourg for the first time, and a woman was elected to parliament.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What were the next two decades like?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A quiet transformation. Charlotte, a poised and popular young monarch, married Prince Felix of Bourbon-Parma in 1919, and their son Jean was born in 1921.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The family became beloved symbols of national unity.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The steel industry prospered, then suffered in the Depression.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1929, a new law made the country unusually attractive for holding companies, the first small step toward its future as a financial center.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I've heard about radio.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1933, Radio Luxembourg began broadcasting from the country, with a powerful transmitter and programs in several languages.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a business as much as a broadcaster, selling advertising across the borders, and in time it became one of the most famous radio stations in Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the shadow of Germany was growing again.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And on the tenth of May, 1940, it fell.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: German forces invaded at dawn, as part of their attack on France and the Low Countries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The country was overrun in a single day.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Charlotte?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Grand Duchess Charlotte and her government escaped across the border into France, then to Portugal, then to London.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She spent much of the war in exile in Britain and Canada, and her BBC radio addresses were heard in secret by people in the occupied country.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They gave courage to many.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And this occupation was worse than the first.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Far worse. Hitler's Germany didn't treat Luxembourg as a neutral occupied country.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It treated it as German. Gustav Simon, the Nazi governor of the neighboring Koblenz-Trier district, was given authority over Luxembourg in the summer of 1940, and his goal was to make the country fully German.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What did that look like?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Thorough, and petty at once. The French language was banned.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: People were told to change their names, street signs were repainted, and even a polite merci had to become danke.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Political parties and trade unions were abolished, and Luxembourgers were declared to be Germans of the Moselle region, who would sooner or later be expected to join the German war effort.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then there was the census.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In October 1941, the Nazi authorities arranged a census with three questions.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Your nationality, your mother tongue, and your ethnicity.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They expected everyone to answer German, which would prove that Luxembourg was a German land.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that's not what happened.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Resistance organizers spread the word quietly, and the answer they urged was Luxembourgish, three times.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More than nine in ten people wrote Luxembourgish on every line.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Germans were furious, and canceled the census.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Jewish community?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It numbered a few thousand before the war, and it was persecuted from the first days of the occupation.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many managed to flee. But more than a thousand were deported to ghettos and camps in the East, and only a small number survived.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then, the summer of 1942.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the thirtieth of August, Simon announced that young Luxembourgers would be drafted into the German army.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within hours, a spontaneous general strike began.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It started in the northern town of Wiltz, and spread to the steel towns, the mines, the schools, the government offices.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Workers walked off their jobs, and trains stopped.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How did the Nazis respond?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Simon declared a state of emergency, and the Gestapo moved in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A special court sentenced about twenty strikers to death, and they were shot within days.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The strike was crushed, but it remains one of the proudest moments in Luxembourg's national memory.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: An act of mass defiance in the middle of a brutal occupation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the draft went ahead anyway.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Around twelve thousand Luxembourgers were forced to serve in the German army.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: About thirty-five hundred deserted or went into hiding, and their families were deported to labor camps in Germany and Silesia.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Somewhere between twenty-five hundred and twenty-eight hundred conscripts were killed or went missing at the front.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's so many families.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It divided families, and left a scar that took generations to heal.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But many Luxembourgers fought on the other side, too.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A small Luxembourg unit served in the Allied armies in Britain.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Charlotte's son, Prince Jean, joined the British Army's Irish Guards, and took part in the advance after the Normandy landings.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And liberation came in September 1944.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: American troops entered Luxembourg City on the tenth, to scenes of wild celebration.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the ordeal wasn't over. In December, Hitler launched his last great offensive in the Ardennes forests, the Battle of the Bulge, and the fighting swept across northern Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the towns in its path.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Wiltz, Clervaux and Vianden were battered.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Wiltz, the cradle of the 1942 strike, was nearly destroyed, and earned the title of martyr town.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And General Patton was there.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His Third Army made its headquarters in Luxembourg City, and from there launched the counterattack that helped save the besieged town of Bastogne, just across the border in Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When the battle ended in January 1945, Luxembourg was free again, but exhausted and scarred.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Patton himself is buried there.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He died in December 1945, after a car accident in Germany.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And he was buried, at his own wish, among his soldiers, in the American military cemetery at Hamm, just outside the capital.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More than five thousand American servicemen rest there today.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So in barely a quarter of a century, Luxembourg had been invaded twice by its giant neighbor.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The old strategy of neutrality, of staying quiet and hoping to be left alone, had failed twice, catastrophically.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The country needed a new way to survive.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it found one. Next, we meet the Luxembourgers who decided that the answer wasn't to hide from Europe, but to help build it.
